segments.vo: In 2011, the space game EVE Online had a problem. Some battles got so big the servers couldn't keep up. Their fix? Slow down time itself, but only in the star system where the fighting was.
Pilots in the battle live through fewer minutes than everyone else. When they fly home, their clocks are behind. More stuff in one place, and time runs slower there.
Now here's the strange part. Our universe does the same thing.

card.title: Is Gravity Just Lag?
card.sub: games, clocks, and why things fall

segments.vo: Put two identical clocks at different heights. The one closer to the Earth ticks slower. Not because it's broken, but because time itself runs slower near something heavy. Physicists have measured this with clocks a millimetre apart. Over a lifetime, your feet age about half a millionth of a second less than your head.

overlays.text: exaggerated for the video · real: ~1 part in 10,000 trillion per metre

segments.vo: So here's the thought. Imagine space as a floor of tiles, and every tile is a little clock, ticking as fast as the computer running it can manage. Now drop in something heavy.

In a game, a region full of stuff costs more to compute, so it updates slower. What if that's what mass does? The slowdown spreads outward, and fades with distance, in exactly the shape Newton found for gravity. This idea isn't new. Brian Whitworth and Alagoz suggested it years ago. We wanted to build it and see if it holds up.

overlays.text: EVERY TILE IS A CLOCK · violet = slower
EVERY TILE IS A CLOCK · violet = slower
idea: Whitworth (2008), Alagoz (2010) · we built it

segments.vo: Now watch what slower clocks do. Here's a line of marchers, walking straight. But the ones closer to the planet are in slower time, so they take their steps a little slower. The line can't stay straight. It swings toward the planet, like a tank when one track slows down.
Nothing in the code pulls anything down. There's no force. The only rule is that each tile runs its own clock. Things fall toward slower time. And that part isn't our idea. It's Einstein.

overlays.text: no force in the code · only local clock rates

segments.vo: If the universe has a tick rate, then nothing can move faster than one tile per tick. Not even light. That might be what the cosmic speed limit really is. So let's race two beams of light. One passes near something heavy. One doesn't.

The beam through the gravity well loses. It's not a trick. Physicists bounce radar off planets on the far side of the Sun, and the echoes come back about a quarter of a millisecond late. And here's the twist: anyone down in the well, timing that light with their own clock, would still measure exactly the speed of light. Only an outsider can see the lag.

overlays.text: real: radar echoes past the Sun arrive ~0.25 ms late (Shapiro delay)

segments.vo: But lag alone doesn't add up. In 1919, astronomers watched starlight skim past the Sun during an eclipse. It bent. If gravity were only slower clocks, it would have bent exactly half as much. It bent twice that. Einstein himself made the half-size prediction in 1911, and had to fix it.

overlays.text: blue: lag only (half)   ·   gold: what we measure
blue: lag only (half)   ·   gold: what we measure

segments.vo: The missing half is space itself. Near something heavy there's more room than there should be. Picture the tiles near the planet quietly splitting into more tiles. A bigger map, packed into the same spot.

overlays.text: THE OTHER HALF · more space near mass

segments.vo: And measurements say the extra space and the extra lag always come in exactly equal amounts, to two parts in a hundred thousand. Here's one way an engine would get that for free. If every tick is a signal that has to travel across its tiles, then more tiles means a slower tick. More space and more lag, always one for one.

overlays.text: A HYPOTHESIS · the tick is a signal
more tiles to cross → slower tick → 1 : 1

segments.vo: There's one big problem left. If gravity were computing load, a complicated object should pull harder than a simple one. A supercomputer should be heavier than a steel ball of the same mass. Drop them.

They fall together. Satellites have tested this with different materials, to one part in a quadrillion. Gravity only sees energy. One idea from this project: maybe extra computation also makes extra space, and the two cancel out exactly, so from the outside, only energy shows. If so, the cancelling has to be perfect.

So. Games slow time where there's too much going on. So does the universe. Clocks near mass run slow, things fall toward slower time, and light takes the long way round. Coincidence, or the same kind of engineering? No conclusions. Just observations.

card.title: No conclusions. Just observations.
